claim: Transcription was proposed to sustain a robust spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC) response.
source: Transcription was also proposed to sustain a robust spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC) response.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature in the abstract.

claim: Under conditions of persistently unattached kinetochores, transcription inhibition with actinomycin D delocalized the chromosomal passenger complex (CPC) protein Aurora B from centromeres.
source: Under conditions of persistently unattached kinetochores, transcription inhibition with actinomycin D, or treatment with other DNA-intercalating drugs, delocalized the chromosomal passenger complex (CPC) protein Aurora B from centromeres, compromising SAC signaling and cell fate.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including immunofluorescence and live-cell imaging.

claim: Treatment with other DNA-intercalating drugs delocalized Aurora B from centromeres.
source: Under conditions of persistently unattached kinetochores, transcription inhibition with actinomycin D, or treatment with other DNA-intercalating drugs, delocalized the chromosomal passenger complex (CPC) protein Aurora B from centromeres, compromising SAC signaling and cell fate.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with ethidium bromide and other DNA-intercalating agents.

claim: Actinomycin D compromised SAC signaling and cell fate.
source: Under conditions of persistently unattached kinetochores, transcription inhibition with actinomycin D, or treatment with other DNA-intercalating drugs, delocalized the chromosomal passenger complex (CPC) protein Aurora B from centromeres, compromising SAC signaling and cell fate.
evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data showing reduced mitotic duration and altered cell fate.

claim: No significant changes in mitotic transcript levels were detected after actinomycin D treatment.
source: However, we were unable to detect significant changes in mitotic transcript levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq and qPCR data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Inhibition of transcription independently of DNA intercalation had no effect on Aurora B centromeric localization.
source: Moreover, inhibition of transcription independently of DNA intercalation had no effect on Aurora B centromeric localization, SAC response, mitotic progression, exit or death.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments with triptolide, a non-DNA-intercalating transcription inhibitor.

claim: Inhibition of transcription independently of DNA intercalation had no effect on SAC response.
source: Moreover, inhibition of transcription independently of DNA intercalation had no effect on Aurora B centromeric localization, SAC response, mitotic progression, exit or death.
evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data with triptolide treatment.

claim: Inhibition of transcription independently of DNA intercalation had no effect on mitotic progression.
source: Moreover, inhibition of transcription independently of DNA intercalation had no effect on Aurora B centromeric localization, SAC response, mitotic progression, exit or death.
evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data showing similar mitotic duration with triptolide treatment.

claim: DNA intercalating agents reduce the interaction of the CPC with nucleosomes.
source: Mechanistically, we show that DNA intercalating agents reduce the interaction of the CPC with nucleosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by EMSA experiments showing reduced CPC binding to nucleosomes in the presence of DNA-intercalating drugs.

claim: Mitotic progression, arrest, exit or death is determined by centromere structural integrity, rather than de novo transcription.
source: Thus, mitotic progression, arrest, exit or death is determined by centromere structural integrity, rather than de novo transcription.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental results showing that transcription inhibition without DNA intercalation does not affect mitotic outcomes.

claim: Transcription is largely repressed during mitosis in higher eukaryotes.
source: Because the half-life of most transcripts exceeds the normal duration of mitosis (typically ~30 min in human cells), the prevailing dogma was that transcription is largely repressed and dispensable during mitosis in higher eukaryotes (Gottesfeld and Forbes, 1997; Konrad, 1963; Martínez-Balbás et al., 1995; Murphy and Attardi, 1973; Prescott and Bender, 1962; Rizkallah and Hurt, 2009; Spencer et al., 2000; Taylor, 1960).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature establishing the prevailing dogma.

claim: The level of chromatin compaction on mitotic chromosomes is highly heterogeneous.
source: Several recent studies have challenged this notion and provided evidence that the level of chromatin compaction on mitotic chromosomes is highly heterogeneous (Nishino et al., 2012), allowing accessibility of some transcription factors and chromatin-modifying enzymes (Burke et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2005; Dey et al., 2009; Egli et al., 2008; Gauthier-Rouvière et al., 1991; Michelotti et al., 1997; Segil et al., 1996; Yan et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A post-translationally modified form of RNA Polymerase II binds mitotic chromosomes at their centromeres.
source: Noteworthy, a post-translationally modified form of RNA Polymerase II that is normally associated with transcription elongation was found to bind mitotic chromosomes at their centromeres (Chan et al., 2012; Dirks and Snaar, 1999; Liu et al., 2015; Molina et al., 2016), suggesting that some transcription is still taking place during mitosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cyclin B1 was proposed to be actively transcribed during mitosis.
source: In line with this hypothesis, the master mitotic regulator Cyclin B1 was proposed to be actively transcribed during mitosis and to be required to sustain a robust SAC response (Mena et al., 2010; Sciortino et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Centromere assembly has been proposed to depend on transcription of centromeric α-satellite DNA.
source: Centromere assembly, which underlies the catalytic mechanism behind the SAC, has also been recently proposed to depend on transcription of centromeric α-satellite DNA and to be regulated by non-coding RNAs (Blower, 2016; Carone et al., 2009; Chan et al., 2012; Du et al., 2010; Grenfell et al., 2016; Li et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2015; Nakano et al., 2003; Pezer and Ugarković, 2008; Rošić et al., 2014; Topp et al., 2004; Wong et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The centromeric localization and activation of Aurora B was shown to be dependent on centromeric transcription.
source: In particular, the centromeric localization and activation of Aurora B, the catalytic subunit of the chromosomal passenger complex (CPC) required for SAC response and error correction during mitosis (Carmena et al., 2012; Santaguida et al., 2011) was shown to be dependent on centromeric transcription (Blower, 2016; Grenfell et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Over 8000 transcripts are expressed de novo during mitosis and mitotic exit.
source: Finally, a recent study using pulse-labeling of nascent transcripts and RNA-seq of mitotic-enriched cell populations reported that over 8000 transcripts are expressed de novo during mitosis and mitotic exit to prepare cells for the subsequent interphase (Palozola et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Cells treated with nocodazole remained in mitosis for 19.2 ± 7.0 hr.
source: Consistent with previous observations in fixed cells (Becker et al., 2010), we found that live cells treated with nocodazole remained in mitosis for 19.2 ± 7.0 hr (median ± SD, n = 386 cells), whereas cells treated with nocodazole followed by actinomycin D persisted in mitosis for only 16.1 ± 5.6 hr (n = 301 cells, p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney Rank Sum Test, Figure 1B,C and Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Cells treated with nocodazole followed by actinomycin D persisted in mitosis for only 16.1 ± 5.6 hr.
source: Consistent with previous observations in fixed cells (Becker et al., 2010), we found that live cells treated with nocodazole remained in mitosis for 19.2 ± 7.0 hr (median ± SD, n = 386 cells), whereas cells treated with nocodazole followed by actinomycin D persisted in mitosis for only 16.1 ± 5.6 hr (n = 301 cells, p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney Rank Sum Test, Figure 1B,C and Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Approximately 90% of nocodazole-treated cells died after a prolonged mitotic delay.
source: Interestingly, approximately 90% of nocodazole-treated cells died after a prolonged mitotic delay, whereas 54% of the cells treated with nocodazole and actinomycin D underwent mitotic slippage (Rieder and Maiato, 2004) (Figure 1B,D and Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 1.

claim: 54% of the cells treated with nocodazole and actinomycin D underwent mitotic slippage.
source: Interestingly, approximately 90% of nocodazole-treated cells died after a prolonged mitotic delay, whereas 54% of the cells treated with nocodazole and actinomycin D underwent mitotic slippage (Rieder and Maiato, 2004) (Figure 1B,D and Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Treatment with actinomycin D compromises the capacity of cells to sustain a prolonged mitotic delay.
source: Thus, treatment with actinomycin D compromises the capacity of cells to sustain a prolonged mitotic delay and interferes with their fate.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the live-cell imaging data showing reduced mitotic duration and altered cell fate.

claim: Slower Cyclin B1 degradation promotes mitotic cell death.
source: The relationship between the capacity to sustain a robust SAC response and the subsequent cell fate after a mitotic delay has been shown to depend on the kinetics of anaphase-promoting complex (APC)-mediated Cyclin B1 degradation, with slower degradation promoting mitotic cell death, and faster degradation promoting mitotic slippage (Brito and Rieder, 2006; Gascoigne and Taylor, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Faster Cyclin B1 degradation promotes mitotic slippage.
source: The relationship between the capacity to sustain a robust SAC response and the subsequent cell fate after a mitotic delay has been shown to depend on the kinetics of anaphase-promoting complex (APC)-mediated Cyclin B1 degradation, with slower degradation promoting mitotic cell death, and faster degradation promoting mitotic slippage (Brito and Rieder, 2006; Gascoigne and Taylor, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cells treated with nocodazole and MG132 increased the mitotic delay relative to cells treated only with nocodazole from 19.2 ± 7.0 hr to 30.1 ± 14.7 hr.
source: Accordingly, cells treated with nocodazole and MG132 increased the mitotic delay relative to cells treated only with nocodazole (from 19.2 ± 7.0 hr to 30.1 ± 14.7 hr, p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney Rank Sum Test, Figure 1C and Video 1), and caused cell death in mitosis in 100% of the cases (Figure 1D and Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Nocodazole and MG132 treatment caused cell death in mitosis in 100% of the cases.
source: Accordingly, cells treated with nocodazole and MG132 increased the mitotic delay relative to cells treated only with nocodazole (from 19.2 ± 7.0 hr to 30.1 ± 14.7 hr, p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney Rank Sum Test, Figure 1C and Video 1), and caused cell death in mitosis in 100% of the cases (Figure 1D and Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Acute SAC inactivation through Mps1 inhibition after nocodazole treatment significantly decreased the mitotic delay from 19.2 ± 7.0 hr to 5.4 ± 2.6 hr.
source: Conversely, acute SAC inactivation through Mps1 inhibition after nocodazole treatment significantly decreased the mitotic delay relative to nocodazole-treated cells (from 19.2 ± 7.0 hr to 5.4 ± 2.6 hr, p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney Rank Sum Test, Figure 1C and Video 1), and caused almost immediate mitotic slippage in 100% of the cells (Figure 1D and Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Mps1 inhibition after nocodazole treatment caused almost immediate mitotic slippage in 100% of the cells.
source: Conversely, acute SAC inactivation through Mps1 inhibition after nocodazole treatment significantly decreased the mitotic delay relative to nocodazole-treated cells (from 19.2 ± 7.0 hr to 5.4 ± 2.6 hr, p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney Rank Sum Test, Figure 1C and Video 1), and caused almost immediate mitotic slippage in 100% of the cells (Figure 1D and Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Proteasome inhibition with MG132 reverted the Mps1 inhibition phenotype, increasing mitotic duration and switching cell fate from mitotic slippage to death.
source: Proteasome inhibition with MG132 reverted the Mps1 inhibition phenotype, increasing mitotic duration and switching cell fate from mitotic slippage to death (p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney Rank Sum Test, Figure 1C,D and Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The ability of actinomycin D to reduce the mitotic delay and induce slippage in cells treated with nocodazole was rescued after inhibition of proteasome activity with MG132.
source: Most important, the ability of actinomycin D to reduce the mitotic delay and induce slippage in cells treated with nocodazole was rescued after inhibition of proteasome activity with MG132 (p≤0.01, Mann-Whitney Rank Sum Test, Figure 1C,D and Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Actinomycin D compromises SAC response in a proteasome-dependent manner.
source: Overall, these experiments suggest that actinomycin D compromises SAC response and the capacity to sustain a prolonged mitotic delay, in a proteasome-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the rescue experiments with MG132.

claim: Cyclin B1-Venus fluorescence decayed very slowly in the presence of nocodazole, likely due to residual APC activity.
source: In agreement with previous reports, Cyclin B1-Venus fluorescence decayed very slowly in the presence of nocodazole, likely due to residual APC activity (Figure 1F) (Brito and Rieder, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 1F and citation to previous work.

claim: Treatment of nocodazole-arrested cells with actinomycin D caused a faster decline in Cyclin B1-Venus.
source: Treatment of nocodazole-arrested cells with actinomycin D caused a faster decline in Cyclin B1-Venus (p<0.0001, Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA), Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 1F.

claim: Cyclin B1-Venus levels in nocodazole-treated cells remained constant for several hours after inhibition of the proteasome with MG132, regardless of the presence of actinomycin D.
source: Interestingly, Cyclin B1-Venus levels in nocodazole-treated cells remained constant for several hours after inhibition of the proteasome with MG132, regardless of the presence of actinomycin D (p≤0.05, ANCOVA, Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 1F.

claim: Actinomycin D compromises SAC robustness and the capacity to prevent APC-mediated Cyclin B1 degradation, independently of de novo transcription.
source: We concluded that actinomycin D compromises SAC robustness and the capacity to prevent APC-mediated Cyclin B1 degradation, independently of de novo transcription.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the Cyclin B1 degradation experiments and the lack of effect on transcript levels.

claim: Addition of actinomycin D for 8 hr in cells pre-treated with nocodazole reduced or abolished pH3S10 accumulation in approximately 17% of the nocodazole-treated cells.
source: In contrast with nocodazole-treatment in which all mitotic cells showed high levels of pH3S10, addition of actinomycin D reduced or abolished pH3S10 accumulation in approximately 17% of the nocodazole-treated cells (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Cells with reduced/abolished pH3S10 after actinomycin D treatment still showed signs of chromosome condensation indistinguishable from neighbouring cells with normal levels of pH3S10.
source: Importantly, these cells still showed signs of chromosome condensation (as determined by DAPI staining of DNA) that were indistinguishable from neighbouring cells with normal levels of pH3S10 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: The observed reduction/abolishment of pH3S10 was not associated with a pre-apoptotic state.
source: Moreover, the observed reduction/abolishment of pH3S10 was not associated with a pre-apoptotic state, as those cells were negative for a cleaved form of caspase 3 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 2A showing absence of cleaved caspase 3.

claim: Cells with reduced/abolished pH3S10 after actinomycin D treatment showed abnormally low levels of total Aurora B and its active phosphorylated form on Threonine 232.
source: In line with the observed reduction/abolishment of pH3S10, these cells also showed abnormally low levels of total Aurora B and its active phosphorylated form on Threonine 232 (Yasui et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 2A and citation to previous work on Aurora B phosphorylation.

claim: In nocodazole- and actinomycin D-treated cells that showed high levels of pH3S10, Aurora B, including its active form, was found displaced along the chromosome arms.
source: Noteworthy, even in those nocodazole- and actinomycin D-treated cells that showed high levels of pH3S10, Aurora B, including its active form, was found displaced along the chromosome arms (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: Actinomycin D compromises normal Aurora B localization and activity.
source: Thus, actinomycin D compromises normal Aurora B localization and activity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the immunofluorescence data showing Aurora B mislocalization and reduced activity.

claim: Addition of actinomycin D for 4 hr to nocodazole-treated cells led to a 45% reduction of Mad1 at the outer kinetochore.
source: We found that addition of actinomycin D for 4 hr to nocodazole-treated cells led to a 45% reduction of Mad1 at the outer kinetochore (Figure 2C,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 2C,E.

claim: Actinomycin D treatment for 4 hr did not affect the kinetochore localization of active Mps1 (Mps1 pT676).
source: Importantly, actinomycin D treatment for 4 hr did not affect the kinetochore localization of active Mps1 (Mps1 pT676; (Jelluma et al., 2008)) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A,B) or the phosphorylation of histone H3 at threonine 3 (H3T3p), a proxy for Haspin activity previously implicated in Aurora B recruitment to centromeres (Kelly et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2010) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Actinomycin D treatment for 4 hr did not affect the phosphorylation of histone H3 at threonine 3 (H3T3p).
source: Importantly, actinomycin D treatment for 4 hr did not affect the kinetochore localization of active Mps1 (Mps1 pT676; (Jelluma et al., 2008)) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A,B) or the phosphorylation of histone H3 at threonine 3 (H3T3p), a proxy for Haspin activity previously implicated in Aurora B recruitment to centromeres (Kelly et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2010) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Actinomycin D compromises the normal localization of Aurora B at centromeres and SAC proteins to unattached kinetochores, independently of an effect over Mps1 and Haspin kinase activity.
source: Taken together, these experiments show that actinomycin D compromises the normal localization of Aurora B at centromeres and SAC proteins to unattached kinetochores, independently of an effect over Mps1 and Haspin kinase activity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the immunofluorescence data showing no effect on Mps1 and Haspin activity.

claim: Addition of actinomycin D for 4 hr to nocodazole-treated cells led to a 22% reduction in phosphorylation levels of Knl1.
source: Consistent with an attenuation of Aurora B activity at centromeres, we found that addition of actinomycin D for 4 hr to nocodazole-treated cells led to a 22% and 43% reduction on the phosphorylation levels of Knl1 and Dsn1 (a member of the Mis12 complex), respectively (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Addition of actinomycin D for 4 hr to nocodazole-treated cells led to a 43% reduction in phosphorylation levels of Dsn1.
source: Consistent with an attenuation of Aurora B activity at centromeres, we found that addition of actinomycin D for 4 hr to nocodazole-treated cells led to a 22% and 43% reduction on the phosphorylation levels of Knl1 and Dsn1 (a member of the Mis12 complex), respectively (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Actinomycin D treatment led to a 29% reduction in total Knl1.
source: Interestingly, we also found a 29% reduction in total Knl1 (Figure 3E,F), whereas total Dsn1, Hec1 (a member of the Ndc80 complex) and CENP-A were unaffected by actinomycin D treatment (Figure 3G,H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Total Dsn1, Hec1 and CENP-A were unaffected by actinomycin D treatment.
source: Interestingly, we also found a 29% reduction in total Knl1 (Figure 3E,F), whereas total Dsn1, Hec1 (a member of the Ndc80 complex) and CENP-A were unaffected by actinomycin D treatment (Figure 3G,H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Perturbation of Aurora B centromeric localization by actinomycin D translates into a local reduction of activity and the consequent decrease in phosphorylation of key Aurora B substrates at the kinetochore.
source: Thus, perturbation of Aurora B centromeric localization by actinomycin D translates into a local reduction of activity and the consequent decrease in phosphorylation of key Aurora B substrates at the kinetochore.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the immunofluorescence data showing reduced phosphorylation of Aurora B substrates.

claim: Actinomycin D treatment for 4 hr compromises the recruitment of Knl1 to unattached kinetochores.
source: Moreover, while actinomycin D treatment for 4 hr does not perturb the normal localization of CENP-A and members of the Ndc80 and Mis12 complex, it compromises the recruitment of Knl1 to unattached kinetochores.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the immunofluorescence data showing reduced Knl1 levels at kinetochores.

claim: Aurora B inhibition in nocodazole-treated cells caused a 38% reduction of Mad1 at unattached kinetochores.
source: We found that, similar to actinomycin D treatment, Aurora B inhibition in nocodazole-treated cells caused a 38% and 28% reduction of Mad1 and Knl1 at unattached kinetochores, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Aurora B inhibition in nocodazole-treated cells caused a 28% reduction of Knl1 at unattached kinetochores.
source: We found that, similar to actinomycin D treatment, Aurora B inhibition in nocodazole-treated cells caused a 38% and 28% reduction of Mad1 and Knl1 at unattached kinetochores, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Constitutive targeting of Aurora B to centromeres by expressing a Cenp-B-INCENP fusion protein was able to rescue SAC response in actinomycin D-treated cells.
source: Importantly, it has previously been shown that constitutive targeting of Aurora B to centromeres by expressing a Cenp-B-INCENP fusion protein was able to rescue SAC response in actinomycin D-treated cells (Becker et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Perturbation of Aurora B localization and consequent decrease in activity at centromeres is the primary effect of Actinomycin D treatment.
source: Overall, these data suggest that perturbation of Aurora B localization and consequent decrease in activity at centromeres is the primary effect of Actinomycin D treatment and this likely accounts for the weakened SAC response due to a downstream effect over Knl1 and Mad1 recruitment.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental results showing Aurora B mislocalization and downstream effects on Knl1 and Mad1.

claim: Aurora B, Survivin and Borealin total protein levels remained unchanged after 4 hr treatment with actinomycin D.
source: Western blot analysis revealed that Aurora B, as well as the total protein levels of the CPC regulatory subunits Survivin and Borealin remained unchanged relative to controls (including inhibition of translation during mitosis with cycloheximide or Aurora B inhibition with ZM447439) after 4 hr treatment with actinomycin D (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Quantitative transcriptome analysis did not reveal any significant changes in annotated or novel assembled transcripts upon actinomycin D treatment.
source: Our quantitative transcriptome analysis did not reveal any significant changes either in annotated or novel assembled transcripts (including all biotypes) upon actinomycin D treatment, ruling out differential gene expression after transcription inhibition during mitosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: Cyclin B1 and all key mitotic regulators, including Aurora B, were not de novo transcribed even during a prolonged mitosis.
source: Importantly, we confirmed that Cyclin B1, as well as all key mitotic regulators, including Aurora B, were not de novo transcribed even during a prolonged mitosis (Figure 4D; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 4D.

claim: Actinomycin D treatment did not reduce the level of centromeric α-satellite RNA.
source: We found that actinomycin D treatment did not reduce the level of centromeric α-satellite RNA (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 4E,F.

claim: Inhibition of transcription with actinomycin D during a prolonged mitosis does not impair normal transcript levels, including centromeric α-satellite RNA, nor the normal levels of CPC proteins.
source: Taken together, our results demonstrate that inhibition of transcription with actinomycin D during a prolonged mitosis caused by persistently unattached kinetochores does not impair normal transcript levels, including centromeric α-satellite RNA, nor the normal levels of CPC proteins.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined RNA-seq, qPCR, and Western blot data.

claim: α-amanitin did not cause any significant effect over Mcl1 transcript levels relative to controls.
source: As suspected, we could not detect any significant effect of α-amanitin over Mcl1 transcript levels relative to controls (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: Treatment with either actinomycin D or triptolide resulted in a 5-fold decrease in Mcl1 transcript levels.
source: In sharp contrast, treatment with either actinomycin D or triptolide resulted in a 5-fold decrease in Mcl1 transcript levels (Figure 5A) and led interphase cells to death within 4–5 hr in the presence of either actinomycin D or triptolide (Videos 1 and 2), suggesting an efficient and equivalent inhibition of transcription in both scenarios.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: Triptolide, but not α-amanitin, caused the degradation of the large subunit of RNA Polymerase II.
source: Finally, we confirmed that, within the time course of our experiment, triptolide, but not α-amanitin, caused the degradation of the large subunit of RNA Polymerase II (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Triptolide efficiently inhibits transcription in living cells independently of DNA intercalation.
source: Thus, triptolide, but not α-amanitin, efficiently inhibits transcription in living cells and it does so independently of DNA intercalation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the qPCR and Western blot data showing efficient transcription inhibition by triptolide without DNA intercalation.

claim: There were no significant differences in mitotic duration between nocodazole-treated cells with or without triptolide (19.3 ± 7.1 hr vs 19.5 ± 5.8 hr).
source: We found no significant differences in mitotic duration between nocodazole-treated cells with or without triptolide (19.3 ± 7.1 hr vs 19.5 ± 5.8 hr, respectively, median ±SD, n = 301 cells, p=0.65, Mann-Whitney Rank Sum Test, Figure 5B and Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: Triptolide did not cause the displacement of Aurora B from centromeres in both fixed and live-cell assays.
source: Triptolide also did not cause the displacement of Aurora B from centromeres in both fixed and live-cell assays (Figure 5D–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 5D–G.

claim: SAC robustness, Aurora B centromeric localization, and the capacity to die in mitosis after a prolonged mitotic delay is independent of de novo transcription.
source: These results, supported by our RNA-seq data, indicate that SAC robustness, Aurora B centromeric localization, as well as the capacity to die in mitosis after a prolonged mitotic delay is independent of de novo transcription.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the triptolide experiments showing no effect on Aurora B localization or SAC response.

claim: Mcl1 transcript levels were only slightly decreased (without statistic significance) after 4 hr of ethidium bromide treatment.
source: Indeed, we found that interphase cells were able to enter mitosis after treatment with ethidium bromide (Video 2). Additionally, Mcl1 transcript levels were only slightly decreased (without statistic significance) after 4 hr of ethidium bromide treatment (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: Cells treated with nocodazole and ethidium bromide spent slightly less time in mitosis when compared to cells treated with nocodazole only (19.2 ± 7.0 hr vs 18.1 ± 5.9 hr), but the difference was not statistically relevant.
source: In agreement, cells treated with nocodazole and ethidium bromide spent slightly less time in mitosis when compared to cells treated with nocodazole only, but the difference was not statistically relevant (19.2 ± 7.0 hr vs 18.1 ± 5.9 hr, median ±SD, n = 386;151 cells/condition, p=0.13, Mann-Whitney Rank Sum Test, Figure 6B and Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: Ethidium bromide caused a significant effect over cell fate after the mitotic delay imposed by nocodazole, causing mitotic slippage in approximately 50% of the cells.
source: However, similar to actinomycin D, ethidium bromide caused a significant effect over cell fate after the mitotic delay imposed by nocodazole, causing mitotic slippage in approximately 50% of the cells (Figure 6C and Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 6C.

claim: Ethidium bromide displaced Aurora B from centromeres in fixed cells, although to a less extent when compared with actinomycin D.
source: Ethidium bromide also displaced Aurora B from centromeres in fixed cells, although to a less extent when compared with actinomycin D (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 6D,E.

claim: DNA intercalating drugs interfere with normal Aurora B localization at centromeres and compromise cell fate after a prolonged mitosis.
source: These data suggest that DNA intercalating drugs interfere with normal Aurora B localization at centromeres and compromise cell fate after a prolonged mitosis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the ethidium bromide experiments showing Aurora B mislocalization and altered cell fate.

claim: Actinomycin D or ethidium bromide-treated NCPs showed ~50% reduction in CPC-CTM binding, when compared to DMSO- or Triptolide-treated NCPs.
source: Consistent with our fixed and live-cell data, actinomycin D or ethidium bromide-treated NCPs showed ~50% reduction in CPC-CTM binding, when compared to DMSO- or Triptolide-treated NCPs (p≤0.05, t test, Figure 6G).
evidence: This claim is supported by EMSA data presented in Figure 6F,G.

claim: DNA intercalating drugs interfere with centromere integrity.
source: Thus, DNA intercalating drugs interfere with centromere integrity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the EMSA data showing reduced CPC binding to nucleosomes.

claim: Control and triptolide-treated cells took a similar time to exit mitosis after nocodazole washout (79.1 ± 28.7 min vs 86.2 ± 31.7 min).
source: We found that control and triptolide-treated cells took a similar time to exit mitosis after nocodazole washout (79.1 ± 28.7 min vs 86.2 ± 31.7 min, median ± SD, n = 116;113 cells/condition, p=0.11, Mann-Whitney Rank Sum Test, Figure 7C and Video 3) without any apparent defect (Figure 7D and Video 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 7C.

claim: Actinomycin D-treated cells showed a significant delay in mitotic exit after nocodazole washout.
source: In contrast, actinomycin D-treated cells showed a significant delay in mitotic exit (Figure 7C and Video 3) and underwent mitotic slippage (33%) or failed cytokinesis (47%) (Figure 7D and Video 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 7C.

claim: Actinomycin D-treated cells underwent mitotic slippage (33%) or failed cytokinesis (47%) after nocodazole washout.
source: In contrast, actinomycin D-treated cells showed a significant delay in mitotic exit (Figure 7C and Video 3) and underwent mitotic slippage (33%) or failed cytokinesis (47%) (Figure 7D and Video 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 7D.

claim: Actinomycin D-treated cells after nocodazole washout showed persistent DNA bridges at the cleavage furrow.
source: Close inspection of actinomycin D-treated cells after nocodazole washout by immunofluorescence revealed persistent DNA bridges at the cleavage furrow (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), which might have accounted for the observed failure in completing cytokinesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The capacity of human cells to progress and exit mitosis, including the completion of cytokinesis, is independent of de novo transcription.
source: Taken together, these experiments indicate that the capacity of human cells to progress and exit mitosis, including the completion of cytokinesis, is independent of de novo transcription.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the nocodazole washout experiments showing normal mitotic progression with triptolide.

claim: The capacity of human cells to sustain, progress, exit or die in mitosis does not require de novo transcription.
source: By combining direct live-cell imaging, while monitoring the efficiency and specificity of transcription inhibition at the whole genome level, we show that the capacity of human cells to sustain, progress, exit or die in mitosis does not require de novo transcription.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental results with triptolide showing no effect on mitotic outcomes.

claim: Actinomycin D and other DNA intercalating agents caused partial dissociation of the CPC from nucleosomes.
source: Actinomycin D and other DNA intercalating agents caused partial dissociation of the CPC from nucleosomes, thereby compromising Aurora B centromeric localization and SAC response.
evidence: This claim is supported by EMSA data showing reduced CPC binding to nucleosomes.

claim: α-amanitin failed to efficiently inhibit transcription even after several hours in mitosis.
source: On the other hand, the slow uptake drug α-amanitin failed to efficiently inhibit transcription even after several hours in mitosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data showing no effect on Mcl1 transcript levels.

claim: Efficient inhibition of mitotic transcription independently of DNA intercalation using triptolide had no discernible effect over Aurora B centromeric localization or SAC response.
source: Most importantly, efficient inhibition of mitotic transcription independently of DNA intercalation using triptolide had no discernible effect over Aurora B centromeric localization or SAC response.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and live-cell imaging data with triptolide.

claim: Centromere integrity, rather than mitotic transcription, is required for proper localization and activity of Aurora B and to mount a robust SAC.
source: We concluded that centromere integrity, rather than mitotic transcription, is required for proper localization and activity of Aurora B and to mount a robust SAC able to sustain mitosis in human cells for several hours in the event of unattached kinetochores.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental results showing that DNA intercalation, not transcription inhibition, affects Aurora B and SAC.

claim: Aurora B activity and its stable association with centromeres are important for normal Knl1 and Mad1 recruitment to unattached kinetochores.
source: Accordingly, we showed that both Aurora B activity and its stable association with centromeres are important for normal Knl1 and Mad1 recruitment to unattached kinetochores.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the immunofluorescence data showing reduced Knl1 and Mad1 levels after Aurora B perturbation.

claim: RNA Polymerase II is generally found displaced from chromatin during prometaphase.
source: Consistent with a global shut-down of transcription during prometaphase (the physiological equivalent of nocodazole-arrested cells), RNA Polymerase II is generally found displaced from chromatin (Hsiung et al., 2016), with the notorious exception of the centromeric region (Chan et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Centromeric transcription is involved in nucleosome disassembly during interphase.
source: Centromeric transcription is involved in nucleosome disassembly during interphase (Boeger et al., 2003) to facilitate the replacement of histone H3 by CENP-A (McKittrick et al., 2004; Tagami et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Experimental increase of α-satellite RNA levels reduced the binding of Sgo1 to nucleosomes.
source: Indeed, experimental increase of α-satellite RNA levels were shown to reduce the binding of Sgo1 to nucleosomes (Liu et al., 2015) and led to problems in chromosome segregation (Chan et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2011), suggesting that the levels of α-satellite RNA must be tightly regulated to ensure a faithful mitosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Experimental increase of α-satellite RNA levels led to problems in chromosome segregation.
source: Indeed, experimental increase of α-satellite RNA levels were shown to reduce the binding of Sgo1 to nucleosomes (Liu et al., 2015) and led to problems in chromosome segregation (Chan et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2011), suggesting that the levels of α-satellite RNA must be tightly regulated to ensure a faithful mitosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The levels of α-satellite RNA must be tightly regulated to ensure a faithful mitosis.
source: Indeed, experimental increase of α-satellite RNA levels were shown to reduce the binding of Sgo1 to nucleosomes (Liu et al., 2015) and led to problems in chromosome segregation (Chan et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2011), suggesting that the levels of α-satellite RNA must be tightly regulated to ensure a faithful mitosis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the cited studies showing effects of altered α-satellite RNA levels.

claim: Regardless of the capacity to detect residual transcription during mitosis, this is not required for human cells to sustain, progress, exit or die in mitosis.
source: Overall, our results demonstrate that, regardless of our capacity to detect residual transcription that might still take place on specific chromosomal loci during mitosis, this is not required for human cells to sustain, progress, exit or die in mitosis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental results showing normal mitotic outcomes with triptolide treatment.
